summary: FireChronicle turns NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS hotspot observations into a burning activity calendar. Land managers, researchers, and emergency response teams can compare fire activity across sensor eras, identify unusually active months, and find recurring peak seasons. The long records for California and Assam span November 2000 to June 2026. Users can draw an area, trace trends back to archived detections, compare recent activity with the same dates in prior years, and export results. In California, calibration lowered mean absolute error from 1,271 to 414 active grid-cell days per month on held-out overlap years.
details:
What FireChronicle does

Satellite sensors see the same landscape at different resolutions and sensitivities. FireChronicle makes their hotspot records more comparable so land managers, researchers, and responders can investigate when activity tends to peak and which months are unusual. The long California and Assam records span November 2000 to June 2026. Thailand and the Laos study area offer shorter monthly records.

How we harmonize the records

The Python and DuckDB pipeline filters NASA FIRMS detections and aggregates unique active 1 km grid cells by UTC day. Overlapping Terra and Aqua detections count once per cell-day in the combined MODIS series. We calibrate eligible platforms against VIIRS Suomi-NPP using seasonal ratios learned from overlapping observations. The calendar distinguishes observed, calibrated, and unavailable months and provides the raw series for comparison.

How we tested it

We hold out each overlap year in turn and evaluate predictions against observed Suomi-NPP activity. MODIS mean absolute error fell from 1,271 to 414 active cell-days per month in California and from 593 to 137 in Assam across 157 overlap months per region. These tests cover years with both instruments operating. Estimates earlier in the archive remain uncertain, and hotspots measure detected activity, not incidents or burned area.

What users can do

The Next.js and TypeScript app uses MapLibre for the hotspot map and Apache ECharts for charts. Users can compare raw and harmonized calendars, see peak seasons and outliers, inspect archived points, draw an area for a local timeline in California or Assam, and compare a recent FIRMS snapshot with matching dates in previous years. The app exports CSV data and PNG calendars. Explicit gaps and provisional feed labels show where coverage limits a comparison.

AI/SI disclosure

OpenAI Codex assisted with planning, code, testing, and drafting the demo script and submission text. Microsoft Edge neural text-to-speech generated the English narration. The video shows captures of the working app and credits NASA FIRMS. Analytics are computed from the cited observed satellite data using the described pipeline.
